sections.h2: How does Nebraska law treat a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
Nebraska treats a quitclaim deed as an ordinary deed for recording and tax purposes, with one rule that sets it apart: a grantor who later picks up more title does not hand that extra title to the person who took the quitclaim. That rule sits in Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-209.

The statute starts from the opposite position. When a deed claims to convey more than the grantor actually owned, any interest the grantor acquires afterward normally flows to the grantee. The statute then carves out quitclaim and special warranty deeds from that benefit. A Nebraska court said the same thing in Troxell v. Stevens (1899), which the legislature's annotations still list under the statute.

The word deed itself is defined broadly. Under 76-203 it covers every written instrument that creates, transfers, mortgages or assigns real estate or any interest in it, apart from wills and leases of one year or less. A quitclaim falls inside that definition, which is why the same recording and transfer statement rules apply to it as to any other deed.

Quitclaim deeds also get their own box on the state's transfer statement. The Department of Revenue's Form 521 lists "Quit Claim" next to warranty, corrective, sheriff and transfer on death as a type of deed the filer can check.

sections.h2: What does a quitclaim deed need before the register of deeds will record it?
sections.html:
The register of deeds will take a quitclaim deed only if it is signed and acknowledged, meets the page format rules, and arrives with a completed Form 521. Each of those points comes from a different statute, so they are easy to miss.

  • Acknowledgment. Inside Nebraska, 76-217 says the acknowledgment must be made or proved before a judge or clerk of any court, a United States magistrate, or a notary public. An officer cannot take an acknowledgment outside his or her territorial jurisdiction.
  • Blank space. 23-1503.01 requires a blank area at the top of the first page at least three inches by eight and one-half inches for the register's recording stamp. If it is missing, the office may add a page and charge for it.
  • Paper and print. The page must be between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches. Text should be black on white paper of at least twenty-pound weight, and the statute presumes a font of at least eight points is legible.
  • Signature. Signatures go in black or dark blue ink, and may be digital or electronic. Each party's name must be typed, printed or stamped under the signature.
  • Transfer statement. Under 76-214, the grantee files a completed statement when the deed is presented. If the grantee does not supply it, the register of deeds shall not record the deed.

The statement is Form 521. The Department of Revenue's form says the deed will not be recorded unless items 1 through 27 are filled in and the grantee or an authorized representative has signed.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a Nebraska quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
The recording fee is $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page, and the documentary stamp tax is charged on top unless an exemption applies. The fee comes from 33-109. The statute also earmarks $2.50 of the first-page fee and 50 cents of each added page for preserving records and modernizing the register's office.

A certified copy of a recorded instrument costs $1.50 per page under the same statute. County sites repeat these numbers. The Chase County register of deeds page, for example, lists the same $10 and $6 figures and the $1.50 certification charge.

The stamp tax is separate. The Department of Revenue's documentary stamp tax page states that as of July 18, 2026 the rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of a thousand. Section 76-901 as now written drops that rate to $2.32 for transfers on or after January 1, 2032.

If you are recording a family quitclaim with no stated price, ask your county register which figure the office applies before you bring a check.

sections.h2: Which Nebraska quitclaim deeds skip the documentary stamp tax?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed is exempt from the stamp tax when it falls into one of the categories listed in 76-902, and the most common one for a house is a transfer inside the family with no real consideration. The statute lists deeds between spouses, between ex-spouses conveying rights to property acquired or held during the marriage, and between parent and child, in each case without actual consideration.

Other exemptions that often matter for a quitclaim include:

  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a recorded deed without extending or limiting the existing interest.
  • Deeds that secure or release a debt.
  • Deeds into a trust, when the same transfer would be exempt if made straight to the beneficiaries. The register of deeds must be shown a signed statement certifying that, and the person signing must keep the supporting evidence for inspection by the Department of Revenue.
  • Deeds from a trustee to a trust beneficiary.
  • Deeds of distribution by a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Deeds to a qualifying 501(c)(3) nonprofit, without actual consideration.

The statute adds a presumption that works against filers: a deed that purports to transfer legal title or a beneficial interest is treated as taxable unless the face of the deed or documentary proof shows the exemption. Form 521 has a line where the filer lists the exemption number, so cite the right one when you submit.

sections.h2: What a quitclaim deed does not do
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed moves whatever title the grantor holds, and the Nebraska statutes reviewed here do not turn it into a title repair tool. Three limits are worth knowing before you sign one.

First, the after-acquired title rule above. If the grantor owned half and later inherits the other half, the person who got a quitclaim does not automatically receive it.

Second, recording priority. Under 76-238, a recorded instrument takes effect as to creditors and later good-faith purchasers from the time it is delivered to the register of deeds, and an unrecorded one is void against a later buyer without notice who records first. Between the two parties, however, the unrecorded deed is still valid. The annotations to that section include a 1896 case, Schott v. Dosh, holding that a quitclaim holder may be a bona fide purchaser, so the deed type alone does not block that protection.

Third, timing of delivery. Section 76-237 considers a deed recorded from the moment it is delivered to the register of deeds, in the order delivered. A deed signed in October but not filed until spring leaves a gap during which a later recorded deed can win.

Nothing in these sections says a quitclaim wipes out a mortgage, a judgment lien or a tax lien. If the house has any of those, a title search is the way to learn what the grantee actually receives.

sections.h2: Selling a Nebraska house that came to you by quitclaim deed
sections.html:
A house that arrived by quitclaim deed can be sold like any other, but the buyer's title company will read the deed chain closely. Questions tend to come from the points above: whether the deed was acknowledged by an authorized officer, whether Form 521 was filed and the correct exemption was cited, and whether the grantor had full title to begin with.

Sellers in this position usually have one of a few stories. A parent put a child on title, a divorce moved a house to one spouse, or an heir signed over a share. Each is a legitimate use of the deed. The trouble starts when the paperwork was done informally and never recorded, or when a co-owner's signature is missing.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and confirm the recording date and book and page.
  • Check that every person who held title signed the deed.
  • Confirm whether any mortgage or judgment against the former owner remains of record.
  • Keep a copy of the filed Form 521 and any exemption statement.

Our team buys Nebraska houses as-is, including homes with messy paper trails. Because the title work decides how fast a sale closes, the sooner you can show the recorded deed, the sooner we can talk through the numbers.

faqs.q: Can I use a quitclaim deed to add someone to my Nebraska house title?
faqs.a: Yes, a quitclaim deed is a recordable deed under Nebraska's definition in 76-203, so it can add a name. It must be acknowledged before an authorized officer, meet the recording format rules, and be filed with Form 521 at the county register of deeds. A deed to a spouse or child with no real consideration is on the stamp tax exemption list in 76-902.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to file a quitclaim deed in Nebraska?
faqs.a: The register of deeds charges $10 for the first page and $6 for each extra page under 33-109. If the deed is taxable, the documentary stamp tax is $3.32 per $1,000 of value as of July 18, 2026, per the Department of Revenue. Family transfers without consideration are exempt under 76-902.

faqs.q: Does the register of deeds check that a quitclaim deed is legally valid?
faqs.a: The register checks format and the transfer statement, not the underlying title. The deed will not be recorded without a completed, signed Form 521 under 76-214, and the page layout rules in 23-1503.01 apply. Whether the grantor really owned the property is a title question the register does not decide.

faqs.q: What happens if I never record my Nebraska quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The deed stays valid between you and the person who signed it, but 76-238 makes an unrecorded instrument void against later good-faith purchasers and creditors who record first without notice. Recording promptly closes that gap.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to prepare a Nebraska quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The statutes do not require a lawyer to prepare a deed, but the acknowledgment, format and tax rules are strict enough that mistakes are common. For anything beyond a simple, debt-free family transfer, ask a Nebraska real estate attorney or a title company to review it.
